author: Carlos Martinez
title: Homestead Miami Speedway iRacing Guide: Setup and Racing Line
description: Master Homestead's tight oval layout with FFB tuning, brake zones, and passing strategy on my MOZA R9 rig.

sections.p: Homestead Miami Speedway is one of iRacing's most physically demanding ovals—tight, abrasive, and unforgiving. At 1.5 miles with a D-shaped layout, it punishes inconsistency and rewards smooth steering inputs. I've spent enough time here losing SR points to learn what actually works, and the difference between guessing your way around and understanding the track's geometry is massive.

I race Homestead on my MOZA R9 (~9 N·m) with a fairly aggressive FFB curve, and the feedback here is almost raw—you feel every bit of tire scrub and corner loading. The setup is tight, the margins are thin, and one sloppy exit costs you three-tenths. Let me walk you through the track, the rig settings that matter, and the racing line that actually works.

Homestead is a D-shaped 1.5-mile oval with Turn 1 on the tight end (roughly 14 degrees), Turns 3 and 4 forming the wider sweeper section, and Turns 2 and 4 being the critical braking events. The banking ranges from ~6 degrees on the straights to ~14 degrees in the turns—shallow enough that you're not riding a wall, but enough that you have to manage momentum carefully.

The track surface itself is abrasive; tire wear is real, and dirty air kills you faster than some tracks. If you're running a stock car or a lighter open-wheel formula, you'll notice the tires getting more aggressive under load as the session ages.

list: Turn 1 (Tight end): Hard braking zone, ~14° banking. Entry speed is ~150 mph; exit is where you lose time if you're sloppy. The rumble strip is your friend—run it hard but don't overdrive the entry.
Turn 2 (Back straight to tight turn): A quick little chicane that catches people off guard. It's a speed control zone; treat it like a drift brake moment if you're left-foot braking.
Turns 3–4 (Wide sweeper): The fastest part of the track. Banking is ~14°, and this is where you carry speed and set up your overtake. A half-car on exit gets you a run down the backmarker.

Main straight and pit entry: The straightaway is long enough to make up ground, but not so long that a 1-mph gain matters. Pit entry is tight and has rumble strips—be smooth on entry or you'll bounce out of line.

sections.h2: FFB and Wheelbase Settings for Homestead

sections.p: On my MOZA R9, I run a notch more overall FFB strength than I do on road courses, because the constant high-speed, low-banking turns demand immediate feedback about edge-of-grip. I'm using roughly 95–100 on overall strength with around 85 on road feel and ~70 on damping. The R9's direct-drive response is crucial here—you need that instant connection to the tire.

The thing about Homestead is that the FFB is constant. You're always fighting some form of understeer or managing oversteer in a shallow-banked turn. Lower damping (compared to my road-course preset) helps me feel exactly when the front is starting to wash; higher damping masks that signal. At Homestead, that signal is money.

sections.tip: Increase road feel to ~85–90 at Homestead. The abrasive surface generates a lot of mid-range vibration, and you want that in your hands—it tells you when the tires are losing their grip circle before you're fully committed to understeer.

sections.p: I also bump sensitivity up slightly (around 1.3–1.4x) to sharpen the steering response. The oval demands quick micro-corrections, and a slower ratio invites oversteer as you're fighting lag in your steering input. Direct-drive helps here; a belt-drive wheelbase will feel sluggish in comparison.

Homestead has two real braking events: Turn 1 and the Turn 2 setup. Everything else is either maintenance braking or coast. The problem is that both braking zones are on the banking, which means your CRP2 load-cell pedals need to be calibrated with a flat pressure curve—none of that progressive curve nonsense.

Turn 1 is the hardest: you're doing ~160 mph on the straight, and you need to scrub that down to ~130 by the apex. That's ~30 mph of energy to kill, and you have about 300 feet to do it. A cold brake pedal will cost you—test your calibration in practice and make sure your pressure curve is giving you linear response from 0 to 100%.

I'm a trail braker here, releasing pressure gradually as I turn in. The banking is shallow enough that you can't just slam on the brakes and point; you have to blend brake and steering input. If you release too early, you'll understeer to the wall. If you hold brake too long, you'll be slow. The margin is tight—maybe 50 ms of adjustment.

list: Turn 1: Full brake pressure from ~700 feet out, release by 50% at apex, trail off to exit.
Turn 2: A lighter braking event; you're already slow from Turn 1. Use it as a precision brake marker, not a power zone.
Turns 3–4: Maintenance brake only—just enough to keep the car settled and bleeding off speed for the chicane re-entry.

sections.h2: Racing Line and Exit Speed Philosophy

sections.p: The racing line at Homestead is all about exit speed because the straights are where overtakes happen. A tenth gained on exit down the backmarker might not sound like much, but by the time you hit the main straight, that's two tenths ahead—and that's a huge gain at this track.

For Turn 1, the line is: enter about 3/4 width outside, clip the inside rumble strip at apex, and power hard to the outside exit. The rumble strip is not your enemy—it's a track feature you use. Don't be afraid of it; hit it confidently and get back on throttle. A timid turn-in costs you corner exit and the following straight.

Turn 3–4 is a flowing sweeper where you want to apex early and carry speed. Don't brake-and-turn; coast and roll through with your hands ahead of your body. The shallow banking means you're working against the tire slip angle more than a high-banked oval, so smooth steering is non-negotiable.

sections.tip: At Homestead, exit speed beats mid-corner speed every time. A tenth slower at apex is worth if you can exit 0.15 mph faster. The straights are your profit centers, not the corners.

sections.p: Homestead is a passing track compared to, say, Martinsville, but it's not a free-for-all. Dirty air is a real thing. If you're running about a car length behind someone down the backmarker, you'll lose ~0.3 mph of downforce (or whatever the equivalent is in your formula—stock cars feel it less, open-wheel feels it more). That might sound small, but it's enough to kill your Turn 1 entry speed.

The overtake setup is: run down the backmarker in Turn 3–4, gain a half-car on exit, and use the main straight as your pass zone. Most passes happen into Turn 1—the braking event is long enough that a run from the backmarker can get you a car length or two. Get even with them before the turn-in point, and you have position into the corner.

Defensively, the line into Turn 1 is your wall. If someone's got a run, block the inside line and hold it through the apex. They'll either back out or hit you—and if they hit you, that's their incident, not yours. Don't over-defend (e.g., don't move twice) or you'll get a penalty, but a single block is fair game.

list: Gain your run in Turns 3–4, not on the backmarker. Dirty air will slow you down if you're glued to the bumper.
Use the straights to close the gap and build your pass, not to complete it. Complete the pass in the braking zones.
If you're being passed into Turn 1, focus on a good exit and make up time on the following straight, not immediately fighting back.
Tire wear matters here—fresher tires on lap 35 beat aged rubber on lap 10. Don't burn them out early in the stint.

sections.h2: Common Mistakes and How to Avoid Them

sections.p: The first big mistake is braking too early on the backmarker into Turn 1. You'll lose two-tenths easy because you're short-shifting your downforce window. Brake hard and late; the rumble strip is there to catch you if you overdrive. Use it.

The second is over-correcting in Turns 3–4 when the car gets loose under braking. Homestead's shallow banking means oversteer happens fast, and your instinct is to crank the wheel harder. Don't. Ease off the brake, let the car settle, then add throttle. A full lock-up at Homestead is a straight-line spin—you've got no banking to support you.

The third is running the car too tight on setup. Homestead rewards a slightly looser car because the low banking means you're managing tire slip angles constantly. If your setup is stiff and aggressive, you'll snap into oversteer mid-corner and lose position. A loose car is forgiving; a tight car is fast but unforgiving.

I start with the default Homestead setup in iRacing and make two key changes: I dial in about 2–3 clicks more wing (front and rear equally) to build downforce for the shallow banking, and I loosen the rear anti-roll bar by 1–2 clicks to kill understeer mid-corner. That combination alone is worth 0.3 seconds a lap for me.

Front wing is your first adjustment knob—add wing if you're losing the front mid-corner, reduce wing if you're spinning the rear on exit. The baseline is usually solid; I rarely need more than a small adjustment. If the car is pushing into Turn 1, add wing. If you're sliding the rear on exit, loosen the ARB before you reduce wing.

Tire pressure is another profit center. Homestead's abrasive surface heats tires fast, so cold pressures should be ~1–2 PSI lower than on a smooth track. Run a short practice session and log your pressures after a few hot laps; aim for them to stabilize in the ~75–80 PSI range (rough numbers, depends on your formula). If they're climbing past 85 PSI, you're building temp too aggressively—either dial in a bit more wing or reduce your throttle input on exit.

sections.tip: Before any setup change, do three laps on a fresh set of tires and log your speed. That baseline tells you if the change helped or hurt. One setup adjustment per three laps—patience wins at Homestead.

sections.p: My Homestead practice routine is simple: 15 laps to learn the line, 10 laps focused on Turn 1 braking consistency, 10 laps on pace, and a final 5-lap race sim with a traffic car ahead. The Turn 1 drill is crucial—that's where the biggest gains hide. Record your brake pressure input and replay any laps where you're more than 50 ms inconsistent with your braking point.

Consistency is the superpower at Homestead. A driver who laps in the 27.1-to-27.3 range will beat a driver doing 27.0-27.5, even though the peak speed is the same. Tight, abrasive ovals don't forgive variation. Your job in practice is to narrow your lap-time distribution as tight as possible—that's how you build SR and win races.

faqs.q: What's the optimal brake pressure curve for Homestead on load-cell pedals?
faqs.a: Use a flat, linear curve. Homestead's shallow banking means you need consistent brake response from 0 to 100% pedal travel. Progressive curves can mask your brake modulation in mid-corner or trail-braking scenarios. Set your CRP2 curve to linear and adjust calibration so 100% pedal equals your target max pressure (usually 70–80 bar, depending on formula).

faqs.q: How much does tire wear affect pace over a 30-lap stint?
faqs.a: Homestead's abrasive surface means you'll lose roughly 0.15–0.25 seconds by lap 30 compared to lap 5 if you're pushing hard throughout. Tire pressure builds faster here than other ovals. If you're managing fuel and tire life, expect a bigger pace loss on older tires—maybe 0.4 seconds by lap 35. Adjust your brake pressure or wing slightly as tires age to compensate.

faqs.q: Should I use left-foot braking at Homestead?
faqs.a: It's optional but helpful. Homestead's shallow banking and tight corners mean precise brake timing matters, and left-foot braking gives you that extra half-second of reaction time in close situations. If you're already comfortable with it elsewhere, use it here. If not, don't switch just for this track—smooth right-foot braking is fine if you're consistent.

faqs.q: What FFB settings help with detecting understeer on the MOZA R9?
faqs.a: Increase road feel to 85–90 (the abrasive surface generates useful mid-range vibration), reduce damping to 65–70 (lower damping preserves the tire-slip signal), and bump sensitivity to 1.3–1.4x (faster steering response helps you catch understeer before it's too late). Test in practice and dial back if the wheel feels twitchy.
